newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Diminished gasoline draw leaves APIs bearish.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Diminished gasoline draw leaves APIs bearish.

text.p: REUTER SURVEY ESTIMATES* ACTUAL STOCKS FOR
FOR WEEK ENDED 07/04/97 WEEK ENDED 07/04/97-CHANGE
DISTILLATE...... UP 1.8 MLN 115,930 UP 0.011 MLN
GASOLINE........ DN 1.5 MLN 204,095 DN 0.137 MLN
UTILIZATION..... DN 0.25 PCT PT 95.6 DN 1.3 PCT PT
*NB - The survey estimate is derived by omitting the high and low forecast and averaging the rest, with a sample of at least six.

A slight decline in demand for U.S gasoline last week left traders with a bearish outlook for energy futures prices, after the American Petroleum Institute (API) reported lower-than-expected draws over the Fourth of July holiday weekend.
"I think we'll get some short-term weakness on this," Al Lindseth, an analyst at GSC Energy.
Implied demand for gasoline stood at 8.557 million barrels per day (bpd), lower than some oil analysts forecast and just under the previous week's high level of 8.57 million bpd.
"It's a little off and that would account for the lack of a bigger draw," said Peter Beutel of Cameron Hanover.

Traders expected a gasoline draw of 1.5 million barrels for the week ending July 4, but API data showed a much milder 137,000 barrel fall in stocks held in primary storage. U.S. gasoline stocks stood at 204.095 million barrels, according to the API.
Gasoline output fell to just under eight million barrels a day, reflecting a 1.3 percentage point drop in refinery use that trimmed run rates to 95.6 percent of capacity.

The lower refinery use could bring relief to oversupplied and underpriced refined products markets, analysts said, although the West Coast's build of 115,000 barrels failed to drawdown supply in a region beset by poor margins.
But U.S. Gulf supplies dropped a sharp 1.2 million barrels, helping prices that have already gotten a boost from heavy refinery buying in the prompt market, traders said.
Analysts said the drop in refinery use came a week earlier than forecast, but that levels were already so high, failure to maintain the brisk pace was natural.

Crude oil stocks also surprised analysts by rising 4.70 million barrels in contrast to expectations of a 2.5 million barrel drop. Crude held in U.S. refinery storage was pegged at 322.66 million barrels, the API reported.
"That crude oil build is disappointing," Beutel said.

The futures market reacted by dropping as much as 15 cents a barrel under the August crude oil contract settle on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX). NYMEX crude oil for August stood at $19.60 a barrel at 1620 PDT.

Distillates also fell below expectations, rising a mere 11,000 barrels last week. But the paltry rise allayed some analysts fears that heating oil stocks, which comprise part of distillate, would enter the U.S. cold-weather season at historic highs.
Stocks, which stand at nearly 116 million barrels, are 17 percent above year-ago, according to analyst Paul Ting of Salomon Brothers.
((--David Brinkerhoff, Los Angeles bureau 213-380-2014))
